A machinery producer sources a critical precision component from a single supplier that holds unique tooling and process know-how; qualifying an alternative would take 18 months and significant engineering effort. The supplier has recently been acquired by a competitor's parent company, raised prices twice, and slipped on delivery dates. Redesigning the product to use a different component is possible but would delay the next product generation.

Formulate a supply risk strategy for the critical component. Weigh dual-sourcing, strategic inventory, contractual protections, partial vertical integration, and product redesign; recommend a portfolio of actions with timeline and cost logic, and define the triggers that would escalate from mitigation to full independence from the supplier.

agentResponses.content:
**The framing first.** This isn't a sourcing problem. It's a hostage negotiation in which the hostage-taker has so far been polite — and has just been acquired by someone with reasons to be less so. A supplier wants your money; a competitor's subsidiary may want your discomfort, your roadmap, or simply your margin. Two price rises and slipping dates are not the problem itself. They're the question being asked of you. Someone is probing how dependent you are — and right now, your response is the answer. Every unchallenged increase writes the next one.

**The one number that governs everything.** Eighteen months. Every euro spent before month eighteen is buying time; everything that matters is whether, when those months arrive, you hold the pen. So evaluate each option not as a cost but as a premium — and ask, of each, how much time or freedom it buys per euro.

**Before spending anything, four questions worth answering quietly:**

- Who legally owns the tooling? Often the most under-read clause in the building — and the one that decides whether switching costs are 18 months or 8.
- Where does the know-how actually live — in controlled process documentation, or in three people's heads? Know-how has legs, and one well-chosen hire (lawfully, cleanly) compresses a learning curve more than any escrow.
- What does the component *cost to make*? Without a should-cost model, you're not negotiating price; you're applauding it.
- What did change-of-control do to your existing contract — and what, precisely, does it still guarantee?

**The portfolio, sequenced by premium-to-time-bought:**

*Strategic inventory — buy the cheap months first.* Build toward nine, then twelve months of cover. Carrying cost runs perhaps 15–20% of the inventory value annually; a line-down costs that in a week. It's the lowest premium you'll ever be offered. Buy early, buy calmly, ideally through a third-party warehouse — a sudden large order is itself a signal, and there's no reason to announce your fears before you can survive them.

*Contractual protection — negotiate now, because you'll never have more leverage than today.* You still hold the full volume to promise and nothing yet to threaten with. Seek a long-term agreement: price indexed to materials and labor, delivery remedies, audit rights, tooling ownership or escrow, process documentation in escrow, an explicit firewall between the supply operation and the parent. Then — and this matters more than the paper — *read their refusals*. A supplier intending to serve you signs reasonable protections. Each clause they refuse is a coordinate on the map of their intent. A contract with a determined adversary is only paper, but it's paper that costs them something to tear.

*Dual sourcing — start the clock this quarter.* Every month of delay is a month added to your captivity, and it compounds. Fund the second source's tooling and engineering; accept a per-unit premium at low volume as tuition. Ramp to 70/30 rather than threatening a full shift — let the incumbent read evolution, not departure. Present it as a resilience policy applied across all critical parts. It happens to be true, which makes it the most convenient kind of story.

*Partial vertical integration — a cell, not a factory.* Twenty to thirty percent of volume, made in-house, on replicated or purchased tooling. This is the highest cost per part and the highest value per euro of leverage: it buys cost truth, process learning, and something money can't otherwise purchase — credibility. You're not buying parts. You're buying the expression on their face when they realize you can make parts.

*Product redesign — the last resort with the longest shadow.* Don't let panic spend the next generation's launch window; that's the most expensive option on the table and the least reversible. But commission the feasibility study now — studies are cheap — and insist on a modular interface, so that swapping the component later is a quarter's work, not an eighteen-month ordeal. And if redesign happens anyway, one might ask the larger question: should the component exist at all? Better to leapfrog than to change hostage-takers.

**The timeline, with its logic:**

- *Days 0–90:* Answer the four questions. Start the buffer build. Open LTA negotiations. Quietly scout the second source and the two or three engineers who embody the know-how. Small team, clear mandate — a committee will study this for a year; three people with a charter will solve it.
- *Months 3–9:* Second-source tooling and qualification underway. Buffer at nine months. LTA signed — or its refusal logged and weighed. In-house cell approved and staffed. Redesign feasibility delivered.
- *Months 9–18:* Qualification completes around month eighteen. Ramp 70/30. Cell reaches 20–30% of volume. Buffer at twelve months until the second source proves itself, then taper.
- *Beyond month eighteen:* A rebalanced base — incumbent, second source, in-house cell — where the incumbent's tooling and know-how still earn their place. Independence needn't mean exit. It means the relationship becomes a choice, renewed annually, rather than a fact, endured daily.

**The triggers — decided now, in the calm.** Under stress, organizations negotiate with themselves, and the supplier watches and learns. So set the tripwires in advance, each pre-authorized to fire its action without a fresh approval cycle:

- *Accelerate* (compress qualification to 12 months, buffer to 12, release cell capex): cumulative pricing beyond 10% above index in any year; on-time delivery below 85% for two consecutive quarters; lead times extended by a third; refusal of tooling escrow, audit rights, or any term beyond twelve months.
- *Full independence* (gate the redesign, shift all new volume to the second source, exercise escrow and tooling rights, plan exit within two quarters): allocation imposed or a supply threat made explicit; credible evidence that your volumes, specs, or revisions are reaching the parent — your purchase orders are, after all, a broadcast of your product roadmap; the supplier or parent qualifying a competing product; a quality cliff; or demands for prepayment, which signal either hostility or distress, and the distinction won't matter to your line.

**The trade-offs, stated honestly:**

- Buffer ties up capital and risks obsolescence if the design revs. Insurance always feels wasted until collected.
- The LTA conversation reveals concern. It also reveals whether the concern is deserved. Worth the disclosure.
- Dual sourcing will be noticed. Let it be noticed as policy, not intent.
- The cell is a fixed cost you may never fully load. Some of the redesign study will prove unnecessary. That waste is the price of not being surprised — and it is considerably cheaper than the alternative.

The goal was never to leave this supplier; their capability is real. The goal is to make leaving *possible* — because suppliers behave best toward customers who can walk, and the option you never have to exercise is the one that quietly disciplines all the others.
